disclaimer: This system provides an informational, model-based prediction only. It is NOT a substitute for diagnosis by a qualified agricultural extension officer, plant pathologist, or agronomist. Always confirm before taking action that could affect a real crop.

Tomato_Healthy.description: The leaf shows no visible signs of disease. Coloration and leaf structure appear typical of a healthy tomato plant.
prevention: Maintain consistent watering, avoiding both drought stress and waterlogging
Ensure adequate spacing for airflow between plants
Rotate crops each season to reduce soil-borne pathogen buildup
management: Continue routine monitoring for early signs of disease
Maintain balanced fertilization based on soil testing

Tomato_Early_Blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, typically appearing on older, lower leaves first as concentric "target-spot" lesions.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern)
Yellowing of tissue surrounding the spots
Lesions starting on older/lower leaves and progressing upward
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant
Remove and destroy infected plant debris at season end
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation away from tomato/potato
management: Remove and dispose of severely infected leaves
Apply an appropriate labeled fungicide following local agricultural extension guidance
Improve air circulation via pruning and spacing

Tomato_Late_Blight.description: A fast-spreading disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, historically responsible for the Irish potato famine. Can destroy a crop within days under humid conditions.
symptoms: Pale green to brown/black patches, often with a fuzzy white mold on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Rapid wilting and collapse of foliage
prevention: Avoid overhead watering and prolonged leaf wetness
Monitor local disease-forecasting alerts, as late blight spreads via wind-borne spores
management: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to limit spread
Apply a fungicide labeled for late blight as soon as symptoms are noticed
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet to reduce spore spread

Potato_Healthy.description: The leaf shows no visible signs of disease and appears typical of a healthy potato plant.
prevention: Rotate crops to avoid continuous potato/tomato cultivation

Potato_Early_Blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani, similar in appearance and cause to tomato early blight, generally affecting older foliage first.
symptoms: Dark brown concentric-ring lesions on older leaves
Premature leaf drop in severe cases
prevention: Avoid water stress, which increases susceptibility
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
Remove volunteer potato/tomato plants and debris between seasons
management: Apply a labeled fungicide at first sign of disease
Remove heavily infected foliage where practical
Maintain adequate soil fertility, particularly nitrogen

Potato_Late_Blight.description: Caused by Phytophthora infestans; one of the most economically destructive potato diseases worldwide, capable of destroying entire fields rapidly under cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark green to brown lesions, often starting at leaf edges/tips
White fungal growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid tissue collapse and a distinctive foul odor in advanced infection of tubers
prevention: Ensure good field drainage and avoid overhead irrigation
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potato plants that can harbor the pathogen
management: Apply protectant/systemic fungicides proactively during high-risk weather (cool, wet)
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Avoid harvesting/handling tubers in wet conditions to prevent spread into storage
